content: A notifiable disease is a condition that must be reported to government authorities as mandated by law. This reporting enables authorities to monitor the disease and provides an early warning system for potential outbreaks. Many governments have established regulations requiring the reporting of notifiable diseases in both humans and animals, particularly livestock. Global Human The World Health Organization (WHO) established the International Health Regulations (IHR) in 1969, which require the reporting of certain diseases to the organization to support global disease surveillance and advisory efforts. The original 1969 regulations focused on three diseases: cholera, yellow fever, and plague. However, the revised International Health Regulations of 2005, which came into effect in June 2007, expanded the scope of reporting. These updated regulations are no longer limited to specific diseases but include a set of criteria to determine whether an event should be reported to the WHO. Animal The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) oversees the global monitoring of specific animal diseases. These diseases are categorized as notifiable to the OIE, ensuring international coordination and response. Australia Human In Australia, the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) was established in 1990. Notifications of notifiable diseases are first made to the relevant State or Territory health authority. De-identified, computerized records are then sent to the Department of Health and Ageing for collation, analysis, and publication. The country maintains a national list of notifiable diseases along with case definitions. Animal The notification of infectious animal diseases in Australia is regulated by the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Forestry. There is a National List of Notifiable Animal Diseases, as well as individual State and Territory Notifiable Animal Diseases Lists. Canada Human Canada maintains a list of national notifiable diseases that must be reported to public health authorities. New Zealand Human In New Zealand, the notification of notifiable diseases is governed by the Health Act of 1956. The country maintains a list of national notifiable diseases. United Kingdom Human The requirement to notify infectious diseases in the UK dates back to the late 19th century. Initially, the list included only a few diseases, but it has since expanded to include approximately 30 conditions. Currently, the notification of infectious diseases in humans is regulated under the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and the Public Health (Infectious Diseases) Regulations 1988. The Health Protection Agency (now part of the UK Health Security Agency) oversees this process. A list of notifiable diseases is maintained for this purpose. Children Specific notification requirements exist for children under the National Standards for Under 8s Day Care and Childminding. These standards mandate that the Office for Standards in Education (Ofsted) must be notified of any food poisoning affecting two or more children on the premises, any case of meningitis, or any outbreak of a notifiable disease as defined by the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 or the Public Health (Infectious Diseases) Regulations 1988. Animal In the UK, the notification of animal diseases is regulated by the Animal Health Act 1981, the Specified Diseases (Notification and Slaughter) Order 1992 (as amended), and the Specified Diseases (Notification) Order 1996 (as amended). While the law states that a police constable should be notified, in practice, a divisional veterinary manager from the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) is informed. Defra then conducts investigations. A list of notifiable animal diseases is maintained for this purpose. United States Human Historically, the list of notifiable diseases in the United States varied by state, as each state had its own laws governing disease reporting. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in collaboration with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE), developed a list of nationally notifiable diseases. These diseases must be reported to the CDC's National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS). In 1990, uniform criteria for reporting diseases to the NNDSS were introduced. The system includes a list of nationally notifiable infectious diseases and case definitions for infectious conditions under public health surveillance.
